item.title: C/C++ Runtime Methods to Determine System Endianness: Union vs. Pointer Casting
item.description:
“C/C++ Runtime Methods to Determine System Endianness: Union vs. Pointer Casting”

What are the established and portable ways to dynamically check if a system is running in Big-Endian or Little-Endian format, and what are the pitfalls associated with type punning versus using newer language features?

Runtime Endianness Detection Techniques

Several approaches can be employed, each carrying different levels of portability, clarity, and susceptibility to compiler optimization.

1. Using C99 Unions for Type Punning (Generally Accepted)

A classic, well-established method utilizes a union to inspect the memory layout of a multi-byte integer. When an integer is written to the union and then read out byte-by-byte, the order reveals the endianness. This is often preferred over raw pointer casts as it aligns better with C99 standards for initialization (though reading from a non-written union member is technically UB in older standards, initializing the union via a member and reading another is often seen as correct for this specific check). If the first byte of the value 0x01020304 is 1, the system is Big-Endian; if it’s 4, it’s Little-Endian.

item.title: Demystifying Amortized Time Complexity: Simple Explanations and Code Examples
item.description:
“Demystifying Amortized Time Complexity: Simple Explanations and Code Examples”

When analyzing algorithms, we often discuss best-case, worst-case, and average-case scenarios. Amortized time complexity offers a distinct perspective, particularly useful for operations that are usually fast but occasionally incur a significant cost. How precisely is this concept defined, and how does it manifest in data structures like dynamic arrays?

The Core Concept: Averaging Over Sequences

If an operation is performed repeatedly—say, a million times—we are less concerned with one exceptionally slow execution and more interested in the total duration spread across all executions. What is the fundamental interpretation of amortized time? It represents the average time taken per operation when a large sequence of operations is considered. The key insight is that infrequent, costly operations can have their expense “diluted” across numerous inexpensive operations. For example, while the amortized time might stabilize at $O(1)$ (constant time), it doesn’t strictly have to be constant; it could manifest as logarithmic or linear amortized time depending on the sequence behavior.
